speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) what is the number of workplace injuries reported in the past five years; and (b) whether the Ministry will consider adopting a system of workplace injury reporting based on (i) diagnosis of a specified list of common work-related injuries requiring medical treatment and (ii) requirement of treatment in a hospital without any time threshold, such as used in the US (Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970), Australia (Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004) and the UK (Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 2013).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The number has been stable over this period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Our reporting criteria are aligned to international practices which focus on reporting injuries that are more serious.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In fact, ours is similar to that of the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This European Union (EU) regulation also requires reporting of any injury that results in more than three days of sick leave.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The reporting regimes in other countries also do not require all injuries to be reported.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For example, in the United Kingdom (UK), beyond the prescribed list of reportable injuries, such as fractures, amputations, burns or blindness, all other injuries are only reportable if the sick leave is seven days or more.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Hence, our reporting regime of three days or more is actually more robust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The UK also requires the injury to be reportable if it results in hospitalisation for more than 24 hours, which is similar to our reporting regime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Our incident reporting criteria of more than three days' sick leave and hospitalisation for more than 24 hours would already cover the more serious injuries that other jurisdictions deem reportable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Hence, our regime is comparable and equally robust as the other developed countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How does MOM know whether there is currently under-reporting of workplace injuries?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, has MOM come across cases where doctors issue less than three days of medical certificate (MC), so that the employer does not need to report the work injury to MOM, and what steps MOM will be taking to address this?

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: First, on under-reporting, we have been monitoring the workplace injuries reporting since the scheme was revised in 2014.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: But, of course, we cannot assume that there will not be any under-reporting.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: But our assessment is that under-reporting is still constituting the minority.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Anyway, under our regime, even if the employers do not report any workplace incidents, the workers themselves can approach and report the injuries or incidents to MOM.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: For cases that are reported to MOM, we will take a look at the situation and then we will take appropriate actions.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: So, within our system, there is already a regime and also a discipline where we can ensure that the workers can report on their injuries even if their employers do not.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: As for the Member's second supplementary question, the issue has been addressed in 2014 when we reviewed and revised our incident reporting regime.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: If any doctors are found to have adopted this practice of issuing two days of MC, then have a break of one day in between, and then issue another one or two days of MC, if we come across such cases, we will investigate.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: And if it is a practice for the employers to avoid reporting the incidents to MOM, we will refer the doctors to the Singapore Medical Council for follow-up actions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can I ask the Minister of State when is the next time this regulation is going to be reviewed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: And during that review, whether MOM will consider adopting a system of workplace injury reporting similar to those of the United States (US), UK and Australia?

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: As I mentioned just now, the Workplace Safety and Health Incident Reporting regulation was reviewed in 2014, which is about three years ago.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We have been monitoring the implementation of this revised scheme and we have found it to be working quite well so far.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: But of course, as a policy matter, policy review is always a work in progress.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We will continue to review and monitor the situation.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: If there is a need to further review it in the future, we will certainly do so.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: When we conduct the next review, we will certainly take reference from international best practices, including the countries mentioned by the Member, that is, the UK, US, Australia and so on.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We will study them, together with other countries' best practices.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We will adopt the most relevant, practicable and reasonable ones to be incorporated and further strengthen our reporting regime.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In regard to near-misses, is the Ministry considering mandatory reporting of near-misses of certain specific injuries since they are quite frequently happening at workplaces?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: And how do we encourage employers to document near-misses or register near-misses to MOM?

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This is, in fact, one of the priorities of MOM going forward, in ensuring better workplace safety and health.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Right now, we have been focusing on the downstream workplace reporting and so on but, actually, the more important aspect is to move upstream, to encourage workers and employers to report near-misses within the company reporting system.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: In the last few months, we have been working closely with the Workplace Safety and Health Council to roll out plans to encourage our employers to take a more proactive approach in reporting near-misses in the workplaces.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: That will be our direction going forward to encourage more proactive interventions upstream to make sure that all the downstream risks could be eliminated.
